questions.stem:
Life is exponential with mean \(\theta\). Use \(e^{-0.4}=0.6703\).
\[
R(t)=\exp(-t/\theta)
\]
What is the reliability at 200 hours?
questions.why: Divide the age by the mean, then use the given exponential. \[ t/\theta=200/500=0.4 \] \[ R(200)=0.6703 \] 0.3297 is the unreliability. 0.4000 is the time ratio. 500 hours is the mean. C. 0.6703

chart.title: Exponential reliability
chart.altText: The mean life is 500 hours. The reliability is asked at 200 hours.

questions.stem:
Three identical units are in active parallel. Any one unit can carry the function. Each has mission reliability \(R\).
\[
R_s=1-(1-R)^{3}
\]
What is the mission reliability of the group?
questions.why: The group fails only when all three units fail. \[ (1-0.60)^{3}=0.064 \] \[ R_s=1-0.064=0.936 \] 0.064 is the unreliability. 0.216 requires all three to survive. 0.600 is one unit. D. 0.936

traps.A: Reports the probability that all three fail.

chart.title: Three-unit active parallel
chart.altText: Three identical independent units each have mission reliability 0.60. Any one can carry the function.

questions.stem:
Each unit runs for the laboratory time below. Multiply by the acceleration factor before estimating the use-condition mean life. There are \(r\) failures.
\[
T_u=nt(AF)
\]
\[
\hat\theta=\frac{T_u}{r}
\]
What is the use-condition mean life?
questions.why: Convert the laboratory exposure first. \[ T_u=6(50)(5)=1500 \] \[ \hat\theta=1500/3=500 \] 50 hours is the laboratory time on one unit. 100 hours divides the laboratory time by the failures and ignores the acceleration. 1,500 hours is the equivalent time. C. 500 hours

chart.title: Accelerated exposure with failures
chart.altText: Six units each ran 50 hours. The acceleration factor is 5. Three failures occurred.

questions.stem:
The sample size for a mean uses the normal factor \(z\), the standard deviation \(s\), and the margin \(E\).
\[
n=\left(\frac{zs}{E}\right)^{2}
\]
What sample size does the formula give?
questions.why: Divide, then square. Do not stop at the ratio. \[ zs/E=2(8)/2=8 \] \[ n=8^{2}=64 \] 8 is the ratio before squaring. 16 is twice that ratio. 32 is half of the required sample. D. 64

traps.C: Uses half of the squared ratio.

chart.title: Sample size for a mean
chart.altText: The normal factor z is 2. The standard deviation is 8. The margin E is 2.

questions.stem: The chart rule in use is that eight consecutive points on one side of the center line are a special-cause signal, even when every point is inside the control limits. What should the team do with the last eight points?
options: Keep running. Every point is inside the control limits.
Investigate. Eight points in a row are above the center line.
Recalculate the limits from these eight points before deciding.
Wait for a point outside the limits. A run on one side is not a signal.
questions.why: The stated rule does not require a point outside the limits. All eight plotted points are above the center, so the rule has been met. Rebuilding the limits from the same eight points would hide the run. B. Investigate. Eight points in a row are above the center line.

traps.A: Treats inside-the-limits as proof of control.
traps.C: Uses the suspect points to redraw the limits.

chart.title: Last eight chart points
chart.altText: The center line is 10.0. The control limits are 9.0 and 11.0. The last eight points are 10.2, 10.4, 10.1, 10.5, 10.3, 10.6, 10.2, and 10.4.

questions.stem:
Cumulative failures in a Crow-AMSAA model scale with total time to the power \(\beta\). Use \(\sqrt{2}=1.414\).
\[
N(2T)/N(T)=2^{\beta}
\]
By what factor does the cumulative failure count grow when the total time doubles?
questions.why: Raise 2 to the growth parameter. Doubling the time does not double the cumulative count when \(\beta\) is not 1. \[ 2^{0.5}=1.414 \] 0.500 is \(\beta\). 2.000 would be correct for \(\beta=1\). 4.000 squares the doubling. B. 1.414

traps.C: Assumes cumulative failures grow in proportion to time.

chart.title: Crow-AMSAA growth parameter
chart.altText: Beta is 0.5. Compare the cumulative failure count at time 2T with the count at time T.

questions.stem:
Each unit has the same expected failures per year. The fleet size is \(n\).
\[
E=nf
\]
How many failures are expected from the fleet in one year?
questions.why: Multiply the fleet size by the per-unit frequency. \[ E=30(0.02)=0.60 \] 0.02 is one unit. 30 is the fleet size. 1,500 divides the fleet size by the per-unit frequency. B. 0.60

traps.A: Reports the rate for one unit.
traps.D: Divides the fleet size by the per-unit frequency.

chart.title: Fleet failure frequency
chart.altText: Thirty units each have an expected 0.02 failures per year.

questions.stem:
Two elements are in series. Element 1 already has reliability \(R_1\). The system requirement is \(R_s\).
\[
R_2=\frac{R_s}{R_1}
\]
What reliability is required of element 2, to three decimal places?
questions.why: Divide the system requirement by the reliability already achieved. Do not multiply. \[ R_2=0.90/0.95=0.947 \] 0.855 is the product of the two numbers in the table. 0.925 is their average. 0.950 copies element 1 onto element 2. C. 0.947

traps.A: Multiplies the system requirement by the known element.

chart.title: Series allocation
chart.altText: The system reliability requirement is 0.90. Element 1 will have reliability 0.95. Element 2 must make up the rest.

questions.stem:
Operational availability uses calendar time, including logistics delay. Uptime is the operating time in the table.
\[
A_o=\frac{\text{uptime}}{\text{calendar time}}
\]
What is the operational availability?
questions.why: Divide uptime by the full calendar time. Logistics delay stays in the denominator. \[ A_o=7200/8000=0.900 \] 0.025 is active repair divided by calendar time. 0.973 removes the logistics delay. 36 divides uptime by active repair. B. 0.900

traps.A: Divides repair time by calendar time.

chart.title: One-period operating log
chart.altText: Uptime is 7,200 hours. Active repair is 200 hours. Logistics delay is 600 hours. Calendar time is 8,000 hours.

questions.stem: Under the rare-event approximation, the top-event probability is the sum of the minimal-cut probabilities. Which cut set should be reduced first?
options: Cut set A. Its probability, 0.040, is the largest term.
Cut set B. A middle term is the best first reduction.
Cut set C. The smallest cut set is the easiest to remove.
None. Reduce the sum, 0.063, rather than one cut set.
questions.why: The largest term contributes the most to the sum, so it is the first reduction. \[ Q\approx 0.040+0.015+0.008=0.063 \] Removing A takes out more of that sum than removing B or C. The sum is the result, not a substitute for choosing a cut set. A. Cut set A. Its probability, 0.040, is the largest term.

traps.D: Refuses to rank the cut sets.

chart.title: Minimal-cut probabilities
chart.altText: Cut set A has probability 0.040, cut set B has probability 0.015, and cut set C has probability 0.008. The rare-event approximation adds them.
